# Results — Study 388 (Lumber-Gold-Ratio)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The folk **lumber/gold ratio**
(Gayed & Bilello, 2015) is said to be a clean risk-on/risk-off switch: when lumber outruns
gold, hold **stocks (SPY)**; when gold outruns lumber, hold **long bonds (TLT)**. We rebuild
that binary rotation switch and race it, on an **excess-of-cash** basis with a 1-day execution
lag and one-way costs, against buy-and-hold SPY, a static 60/40 SPY/TLT blend, and a
**same-exposure random-timing** control. The decisive question is not the switch's own Sharpe
(a bond sleeve can flatter it in a falling-rate regime) but whether the *timing* beats the
passive mix by more than luck. Offline & deterministic; run `python examples/verify.py` to
reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes — WOOD, GLD, SPY, TLT, ^IRX (public, no key) |
| Window | 2008-06-25 → 2026-06-22 (**4,525** trading days; **18.0** years) |
| Signal | standardised deviation of the *log* WOOD/GLD ratio from its 60-day trailing mean |
| Switch | z > 0 (ratio stretched-high → risk-on) ⇒ SPY; else ⇒ TLT; neutral 50/50 while warming up |
| Entry / costs | 1-day execution lag; 5 bps one-way cost on every rotation (≈609 rotations) |
| Cash leg | ^IRX 13-week T-bill yield / 252 (excess-of-cash for every book) |
| Fingerprint | `3106452822a7` (equity column) |

> **Proxy caveat (named on the Signal axis).** The classic lumber/gold ratio is built from
> *lumber futures* (Yahoo `LBS=F`), but that contract was **discontinued in May 2023** (replaced
> by the smaller `LBR` future with little free history), so a current-window study to 2026 cannot
> use it. We therefore use the **WOOD** timber/forestry-equity ETF as a transparent, continuous
> **lumber proxy** — a basket of forestry/timber *equities*, not the cash lumber price. WOOD is
> itself an equity (it co-moves with stocks), which if anything *flatters* a "risk-on" reading.
> The verdict does **not** hinge on the proxy: the switch is beaten by a passive mix and shows no
> timing edge over a random control, which the cash-lumber series would not rescue.

## The race — does the rotation switch beat doing nothing?

Excess-of-cash basis (every sleeve is risky, so we compare excess-of-cash to keep one clock).
Net of a 5 bps one-way cost on every rotation. `t_excess` is the Newey-West HAC *t* that each
book's own excess-of-cash daily mean differs from zero.

| book | ann. return | Sharpe (excess) | max DD | % in stocks | HAC *t* (own excess) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **lumber/gold switch** | **+5.21%** | **0.32** | **−59.5%** | 53.2% | 1.43 |
| buy-and-hold SPY | +12.16% | 0.61 | −47.6% | 100.0% | 3.01 |
| **static 60/40 SPY/TLT** | +9.36% | **0.71** | −27.2% | 60.0% | 3.24 |
| random-timing (same exposure) | +3.67% | 0.22 | −45.8% | 53.2% | 1.04 |

Read it carefully. The switch's own Sharpe is **0.32** — and the obvious passive mix it must
beat, a **static 60/40**, scores **0.71** with a *shallower* drawdown (−27% vs −60%). The switch
does not even clear its own risk-free t-bar convincingly (t = 1.43), and it spends 53% of days in
stocks — so it is essentially a *worse-timed* 50/50 blend. Far from a defensive crown jewel, the
rotation **destroys** value versus the static blend.

## Head-to-head — the decisive inference

The decisive number is the HAC *t* that the switch's **net excess-of-cash daily return exceeds
the benchmark's** — with block-bootstrap CIs on the mean daily difference (in bps/day).

| switch minus … | HAC *t* | 95% block-bootstrap CI (bps/day) |
|---|--:|--:|
| buy-and-hold SPY | **−1.55** | — |
| **static 60/40** | **−1.06** | **[−3.79, +1.15]** |
| random-timing (same exposure) | **+0.25** | **[−2.65, +3.51]** |

Both head-to-heads that matter come back empty. Versus the **60/40** the *t* is **negative**
(−1.06) and the CI straddles zero — the switch is, if anything, *worse* than the passive mix. The
cleanest test of the folklore is **switch vs random rotation with the same stock exposure**: if
the lumber/gold ratio carried regime information, the real switch would beat a coin that holds
bonds on the *same number* of random days. It does **not** — the *t* is **+0.25**, a dead heat,
with a CI symmetric around zero. **There is no timing information in the ratio.**

## Robustness — no lookback or threshold rescues it

| config | switch Sharpe | *t* vs 60/40 | *t* vs random |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| lookback 40, z>0 | 0.35 | −0.89 | 0.36 |
| **lookback 60, z>0** (base) | 0.32 | −1.06 | 0.25 |
| lookback 90, z>0 | 0.36 | −0.88 | 1.75 |
| lookback 60, z>+0.5 | 0.30 | −1.19 | 0.40 |
| lookback 60, z>−0.5 | 0.54 | +0.06 | 0.59 |

Across every lookback and threshold the switch's *t* vs 60/40 is **negative or zero** and its
*t* vs random never clears 2. The only config that lifts the switch Sharpe to 0.54 is **z>−0.5**
— i.e. holding stocks **almost always** (a 90%-equity book that simply rides the SPY up-drift),
which is no longer a "rotation" at all and still doesn't beat random timing (t = 0.59). There is
no corner of the parameter grid where the *timing* adds value.

## Synthetic null + positive control — the engine is faithful

A deterministic offline tape with a single planted-edge knob `pred_r` (the forward link between
the lagged lumber/gold z-score and the next day's equity-minus-bond spread):

| planted `pred_r` | switch Sharpe | *t* vs 60/40 | *t* vs random | verdict |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (null — no link) | −0.14 | **+0.56** | +2.56 | not significant on 60/40 |
| **+0.15** (folklore-consistent edge) | +11.25 | **+41.1** | +29.8 | significant — recovered |

With **no** planted link the decisive `t` vs 60/40 stays at **+0.56** — the inference does **not**
manufacture significance from the null tape. (The single shared `rand_seed` makes the null's
*t* vs random wander to ~2.5 on this one draw — a reminder that the random control is one draw,
which is why the **60/40** head-to-head is the decisive axis.) When a genuine
folklore-consistent edge is planted (`pred_r=+0.15`), the same machinery lights up to **t = 41** —
so the engine *would* find a real lumber/gold timing edge if one existed. On the real tape it
finds **t = −1.06**: not absence of power, but absence of edge.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The folklore says a high lumber/gold ratio is a risk-on green light. On 18
  years of real data the switch it implies is **beaten by a static 60/40** (Sharpe 0.32 vs 0.71,
  *t* vs 60/40 = **−1.06**) and **ties a same-exposure coin** (*t* vs random = **+0.25**). The
  synthetic control confirms the test has power (it recovers a planted edge at t = 41), so the
  flat real-tape result is **no signal**, not low power.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** ~**609 rotations** in 18 years, each a whole-book one-way trade, for a
  book that under-performs the passive mix it is supposed to improve and carries a **−59.5%**
  drawdown (twice the 60/40's). After costs there is nothing to deploy — a defensive switch that is
  *more* drawdown-prone than buy-and-hold is the opposite of what was advertised.
- **Beats 60/40? — BUSTED.** The whole appeal of an intermarket switch is that the *timing* earns
  its keep over the obvious passive stock/bond blend. It does not: the head-to-head *t* is
  **negative**, the bootstrap CI straddles zero, and no lookback/threshold flips it positive. The
  lumber/gold ratio is a vivid macro story that, as a tradable rotation rule, **loses to 60/40 and
  ties a dice roll**.
